av_event.line_text: Oh no, is he alright now?
av_event.what: Jaspal's smile drops and his eyes move off the screen to the small framed photo of an older couple on the bookshelf behind him. He holds that look for about two seconds before turning back to the camera, and his voice is quieter than before as he asks the question.

text:
B: Hiya, can you hear me alright? I'm Craig, I'm in Warrington.
A: Hiya mate, yeah, loud and clear. Jaspal, Derby. I clocked the Wolves magnet on your fridge, so I'm guessing rugby league?
B: Rugby league, yeah, Warrington Wolves, born and bred. And I clocked your Derby shirt, so I'm guessing you suffer.
A: Suffer is the word, mate. I go with my cousin a few times a season and we moan about the board from the car park all the way down the A38. It's basically therapy. Do you follow the football as well?
B: Casually. Mainly so I've got something to say to clients, if I'm honest. I'm in sales, flooring, so half my day is "did you see the match?" with a facilities manager.
A: Ha, that's genius, that. I'm a teacher, Business and Economics, and I do the exact same with the lads at the back. You get them on the football and then you sneak inflation in.
B: Sneak inflation in, I like that. There was a dog's tail in your photo, wasn't there? Bottom corner.
A: That's Biscuit. My partner's dog, technically, but I do the walks. Reluctantly.
B: You're joking. Ours is called Biscuit. Cockapoo.
A: No way. Ours is a cocker spaniel, old lad now. Does yours eat socks?
B: Ate one last week! I was in the garden at ten at night with a torch.
A: Mate, same, we've had the vet bill and everything. It's like there's a national Biscuit conspiracy.
B: There must be, because that's three now. I had a call earlier with a physio, Gemma, from near Nottingham, and hers is a Biscuit as well.
A: Hang on, hang on. My partner's called Gemma. And she's a physio.
B: Stop it.
A: Swear down. Royal Derby, though, not Nottingham. Did she say anything about a handsome teacher?
B: Ha, she said she was married to a Dan, so I'd hope it's not her, mate.
A: I'd hope so too! Nine years and we're not married, so if she's gone and married a Dan behind my back I've got questions. Sorry, go on, what were you saying about work?
B: No, just the sales. Cheshire, Merseyside, Manchester, I'm on the M62 most of the week. Did three hundred miles this week. Five-a-side on a Wednesday's about the only fixed thing, and even that I sort of hobble round now with my ankle.
A: Wednesday five-a-side! Same night, me. I'm mostly there for the pint, to be fair. I say I'm a holding midfielder, which means I hold my position because I can't run.
B: Ha, that's me now. Since forty I've slowed right down. Cut back on the midweek beers and all. My dad had a heart scare a few months ago, and it sort of makes you think, you know.
A: Oh no, is he alright now?
B: He's doing better. On tablets, walking every day, my mum's got him on porridge, which he's not happy about.
A: Porridge, ha. My mum would sooner die than give my dad porridge. Everything's rice and bolani and ghee in our house. She sends me home with tubs every Sunday.
B: Bolani? What's that?
A: Afghan flatbread, stuffed, potato and leek usually. We're Afghan Sikh, came over when I was nine. Honestly, I make a decent karahi, but I can't touch my mum's bolani.
B: That sounds unbelievable. I'm a slow-cooker chilli man myself. Kerry does most of the teas, I do the Sunday roast, and the barbecue if there's any sun.
A: Barbecue the second it hits twelve degrees, I bet.
B: Fourteen. I'm not an animal.
A: Fair. Right, important question, what car are you getting next? Because I'm fancying one and I need talking out of it.
B: Oh, don't get me started, I'm choosing my next lease right now...
